citation.title: Unbiased Estimation of the Average Treatment Effect in Cluster-Randomized Experiments

standing_assumptions:
Finite-population, design-based potential-outcomes setting; the only randomness is the allocation of clusters. Transcribed from the page images.

(S1) p. 41 (PDF p. 3), Section 2: 'Define treatment indicator $D_i\in\{0,1\}$ for units $i\in 1,2,\ldots,N$ such that $D_i=1$ when unit $i$ receives the treatment and $D_i=0$ otherwise. Assuming that the stable unit treatment value assumption (Rubin 1978, 2005) holds, let $Y_{1i}$ be the potential outcome if unit $i$ is exposed to the treatment, and let $Y_{0i}$ be the potential outcome if unit $i$ is not exposed to the treatment. The observed experimental outcome $Y_i$ may be expressed as a function of the potential outcomes and the assigned treatment: $Y_i=D_iY_{1i}+(1-D_i)Y_{0i}$. The causal effect of the treatment on unit $i$, $\tau_i$, is defined as the difference between the two potential outcomes for unit $i$: $\tau_i\equiv Y_{1i}-Y_{0i}$. And, by definition the ATE, denoted $\Delta$, is the average value of $\tau_i$ for all units $i$. Under this model, the only random component of the experiment is the allocation of units to treatment and control groups.' Then $\Delta=\frac{\sum_{i=1}^N(Y_{1i}-Y_{0i})}{N}=\frac1N\left[\sum_{i=1}^NY_{1i}-\sum_{i=1}^NY_{0i}\right]=\frac1N[Y_1^T-Y_0^T]$, 'where $Y_1^T$ is the sum of potential outcomes if in the treatment condition and $Y_0^T$ is the sum of potential outcomes if in the control condition', and equation (1): $\hat\Delta=\frac1N\left[\widehat{Y_1^T}-\widehat{Y_0^T}\right]$.

(S2) p. 42 (PDF p. 4), Section 2: 'Formally, the bias of an estimator is the difference between the expected value of the estimator (over all randomizations) and the parameter of interest. If the estimators $\widehat{Y_0^T}$ and $\widehat{Y_1^T}$ are unbiased, the corresponding estimator of $\Delta$ is also unbiased since $\mathrm{E}[\hat\Delta]=\frac1N\left[\mathrm{E}\left[\widehat{Y_1^T}\right]-\mathrm{E}\left[\widehat{Y_0^T}\right]\right]=\frac1N[Y_1^T-Y_0^T]=\Delta$.' Footnote 3: 'Throughout, we use the term random allocation to refer to the assignment of a fixed number of units (or clusters) to treatment and a fixed number to control, following the terminology of Lachin (1988).'

(S3) p. 44 (PDF p. 6), Section 3.2 (the cluster design every result below inherits): 'Formally, suppose each cluster $j=1,2,\ldots,M$ is assigned to either treatment or control. Define $m_t$ and $M$ as (fixed) integers such that $0<m_t<M$. Now $m_t$ clusters are randomly assigned to treatment ($D_j=1$) and the remaining $m_c=M-m_t$ clusters are assigned to control ($D_j=0$). Define $J_0$ as the set of all $j$ such that $D_j=0$ and $J_1$ as the set of all $j$ such that $D_j=1$. Let $Y_{0ij}$ be the response of the $i^{th}$ individual in the $j^{th}$ cluster if the cluster is assigned to control and let $Y_{1ij}$ be the response of the $i^{th}$ individual in the $j^{th}$ cluster if the cluster is assigned to treatment. Let $n_j$ be the number of individuals in the $j^{th}$ cluster. Note that all individuals have the same probability $m_t/M$ of entering treatment.' Also p. 44: '$n_t=\sum_{j\in J_1}n_j$ and $n_c=\sum_{j\in J_0}n_j$ are no longer fixed numbers ... but are now random variables.'

(S4) p. 48 (PDF p. 10), Section 4 (cluster totals): 'Define $Y^T_{0j}=\sum_{i=1}^{n_j}Y_{0ij}$ as the sum of responses of the individuals in the $j^{th}$ cluster if assigned to control and $Y^T_{1j}=\sum_{i=1}^{n_j}Y_{1ij}$ as the sum of responses of the individuals in the $j^{th}$ cluster if assigned to treatment. ... The observed cluster total for cluster $j$, $Y^T_j$, may be expressed as: $Y^T_j=D_jY^T_{1j}+(1-D_j)Y^T_{0j}$.' and '$\Delta=\frac{\sum_{j=1}^M\sum_{i=1}^{n_j}(Y_{1ij}-Y_{0ij})}{\sum_{j=1}^M\sum_{i=1}^{n_j}1}=\frac{\sum_{j=1}^MY^T_{1j}-\sum_{j=1}^MY^T_{0j}}{\sum_{j=1}^Mn_j}=\frac1N[Y^T_1-Y^T_0]$.'

(S5) p. 50 (PDF p. 12), Section 4.2 (finite population moments, divisor $M$): 'given features $v_j$ and $w_j$ for $j\in 1,\ldots,M$, finite population variance $\sigma^2(v_j)=\frac1M\sum_{j=1}^M\left(v_j-\frac1M\sum_{j=1}^Mv_j\right)^2$ and finite population covariance $\sigma(v_j,w_j)=\frac1M\sum_{j=1}^M\left(v_j-\frac1M\sum_{j=1}^Mv_j\right)\left(w_j-\frac1M\sum_{j=1}^Mw_j\right)$.'

(S6) Reading used throughout, implicit in the paper and not printed in these words: 'randomly assigned' means that every set $J_1$ of $m_t$ of the $M$ clusters is equally likely (complete randomization of clusters); $\mathrm{E}$, $\mathrm{V}$ and $\mathrm{Cov}$ of estimators are taken over that distribution with the potential outcomes and cluster sizes fixed; $N=\sum_{j=1}^Mn_j$ and every $n_j\geq1$. $Y_{ij}$ denotes the observed outcome of individual $i$ in cluster $j$. In Appendix C (p. 72, PDF p. 34) the paper also writes $\mathrm{E}[\cdot]$ and an overline for the average over the $M$ clusters of a cluster-indexed quantity, and writes the cluster totals as $Y^T_{j0},Y^T_{j1}$ where the main text writes $Y^T_{0j},Y^T_{1j}$. The paper has no numbered theorems; its results are numbered equations.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Introduction, unnumbered sentence 'Estimators that are asymptotically biased are guaranteed to be relatively inefficient for a sufficiently large sample size'; repeated in the opening paragraph of Section 3
canonical_claim.statement:
Printed statements refuted. p. 40: 'In choosing an estimator, researchers often consider efficiency (typically mean square error) to be of paramount importance. However, as we show below, the bias of estimators such as the difference-in-means estimator may not diminish with increasing study size under common designs. Estimators that are asymptotically biased are guaranteed to be relatively inefficient for a sufficiently large sample size, and we provide an empirical example where bias is critical in undermining the relative efficiency of common estimators.' p. 42: 'Third, the derivations will help us to identify conditions under which common estimators are not consistent and, hence, asymptotically inefficient.'

Counterexample (validator, exact rational arithmetic). Random allocation of clusters with $M=3$, $m_t=1$, $m_c=2$; cluster sizes $(n_1,n_2,n_3)=(1,2,4)$, $N=7$; individual control potential outcomes $(0)$, $(1,0)$, $(1,0,0,0)$ in clusters 1, 2, 3 and all individual treatment potential outcomes equal to $0$, so that $(Y^T_{01},Y^T_{02},Y^T_{03})=(0,1,1)$, $(Y^T_{11},Y^T_{12},Y^T_{13})=(0,0,0)$ and $\Delta=-2/7$. The three assignments (treated cluster 1, 2 or 3) each have probability $1/3$. Write $\mathrm{MSE}(\hat\theta)=\mathrm{E}[(\hat\theta-\Delta)^2]$. Then:
(i) $\widehat{\Delta_S}$ (equation 6) takes the values $(-1/3,-1/5,-1/3)$; $\mathrm{E}[\widehat{\Delta_S}]=-13/45$, its bias is $-1/315\neq0$, and $\mathrm{MSE}(\widehat{\Delta_S})=131/33075$.
(ii) $\widehat{\Delta_{HT}}$ (equation 13) takes the values $(-3/7,-3/14,-3/14)$; $\mathrm{E}[\widehat{\Delta_{HT}}]=\Delta$ and $\mathrm{MSE}(\widehat{\Delta_{HT}})=1/98$.
(iii) For every fixed real $k$, $\widehat{\Delta_{R1}}$ (equations 20-21) takes the values $\left(-\frac37+\frac67k,\ -\frac3{14}+\frac3{14}k,\ -\frac3{14}-\frac{15}{14}k\right)$, is unbiased, and $\mathrm{MSE}(\widehat{\Delta_{R1}})=\frac1{98}-\frac6{49}k+\frac9{14}k^2=\frac3{686}+\frac9{14}\left(k-\frac2{21}\right)^2\geq\frac3{686}$, with equality iff $k=2/21$, which equals $k_{optim*}$ of Section 5.3 for this population ($\sigma^2(n_j)=14/9$, $\sigma(n_j,Y^T_{0j})=4/9$, $\sigma(n_j,Y^T_{1j})=0$).
(iv) $\frac{131}{33075}<\frac3{686}<\frac1{98}$: the biased difference-in-means estimator has strictly smaller mean squared error than the Horvitz-Thompson estimator and than the Des Raj estimator with any fixed $k$.
(v) For every positive integer $h$, copy each individual $h$ times within its own cluster (the growth scheme of Section 3.3, p. 47, and Figure 1, Panel B): $n^{(h)}_j=hn_j$, $Y^{T,(h)}_{0j}=hY^T_{0j}$, $Y^{T,(h)}_{1j}=hY^T_{1j}$, $N_h=7h$, with $M=3$, $m_t=1$, $m_c=2$ unchanged. Then $\Delta$, the three values of $\widehat{\Delta_S}$, of $\widehat{\Delta_{HT}}$ and of $\widehat{\Delta_{R1}}$ (for each fixed $k$), and therefore (i)-(iv), are the same for every $h$, while $N_h\to\infty$. In particular, for every $h$: the bias of $\widehat{\Delta_S}$ is $-1/315$; $P(|\widehat{\Delta_S}-\Delta|>1/25)=1$ (so $\widehat{\Delta_S}$ is not consistent along this sequence); and $\mathrm{MSE}(\widehat{\Delta_S})<\mathrm{MSE}(\widehat{\Delta_{R1}})$ for every real $k$, including $k=0$ (the HT estimator), where $k$ may also depend on $h$.
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: Difference-in-means estimator, equation (6), p. 44 (PDF p. 6): $\widehat{\Delta_S}=\frac1N\left[\widehat{Y^T_{1,S}}-\widehat{Y^T_{0,S}}\right]=\frac{\sum_{j\in J_1}\sum_{i=1}^{n_j}Y_{ij}}{\sum_{j\in J_1}n_j}-\frac{\sum_{j\in J_0}\sum_{i=1}^{n_j}Y_{ij}}{\sum_{j\in J_0}n_j}$. Horvitz-Thompson estimator, equations (11)-(13), pp. 48-49 (PDF pp. 10-11): $\widehat{Y^T_{0,HT}}=\frac M{m_c}\sum_{j\in J_0}Y^T_j$, $\widehat{Y^T_{1,HT}}=\frac M{m_t}\sum_{j\in J_1}Y^T_j$, $\widehat{\Delta_{HT}}=\frac1N\left[\widehat{Y^T_{1,HT}}-\widehat{Y^T_{0,HT}}\right]=\frac MN\left[\frac1{m_t}\sum_{j\in J_1}Y^T_j-\frac1{m_c}\sum_{j\in J_0}Y^T_j\right]$. Des Raj difference estimator, equations (20)-(21) and the display after (22), p. 54 (PDF p. 16): $\widehat{Y^T_{0,R1}}=\frac M{m_c}\sum_{j\in J_0}(Y^T_j-k(n_j-N/M))$, $\widehat{Y^T_{1,R1}}=\frac M{m_t}\sum_{j\in J_1}(Y^T_j-k(n_j-N/M))$, $\widehat{\Delta_{R1}}=\frac1N\left[\widehat{Y^T_{1,R1}}-\widehat{Y^T_{0,R1}}\right]$, with $k$ a constant fixed before analysis; differenced variable $U^T_j=Y^T_j-k(n_j-N/M)$ (p. 54), with potential versions $U^T_{0j}=Y^T_{0j}-k(n_j-N/M)$ and $U^T_{1j}=Y^T_{1j}-k(n_j-N/M)$ (used on pp. 55-56; the first display of Section 5.3, p. 56, shows $U^T_{0j}-\overline{U^T_{0j}}=Y^T_{0j}-k(n_j-N/M)-\overline{Y^T_{0j}}$). Mean squared error is not defined by a formula in the paper (p. 40 says 'efficiency (typically mean square error)'); it is taken as $\mathrm{E}[(\hat\theta-\Delta)^2]$ over the randomization distribution. Consistency: p. 45 (PDF p. 7), 'The estimator $\widehat{\Delta_S}$ is said to be a consistent estimator of $\Delta$ if $\widehat{\Delta_S}\xrightarrow{p}\Delta$ (converges in probability) as $h\to\infty$.' $k_{optim_c}=\frac{\sigma(n_j,Y^T_{0j})}{\sigma^2(n_j)}$ (equation 26, p. 57, PDF p. 19); $k_{optim_t}=\sigma(n_j,Y^T_{1j})/\sigma^2(n_j)$ and $k_{optim*}=m_tk_{optim_c}/M+m_ck_{optim_t}/M$ (p. 57).

The paper names no comparator for 'relatively inefficient'; the validator used the paper's own unbiased estimators (HT and fixed-k Des Raj). Not established and not part of the target: domination of every unbiased estimator, of Des Raj with arm-specific coefficients or extra covariates, or anything about the application's RMSE rankings. canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Introduction, unnumbered sentence 'Estimators that are asymptotically biased are guaranteed to be relatively inefficient ...' (and the Section 3 roadmap sentence), as corrected
canonical_claim.statement:
Corrected wording (the validator's smallest repair). p. 40: 'Persistent asymptotic bias contributes a nonvanishing squared-bias term to mean squared error and can undermine relative efficiency. It guarantees eventual mean-squared-error inferiority to a specified comparator when that comparator's mean squared error tends to zero.' p. 42: 'Third, the derivations will help us to identify conditions under which common estimators are not consistent; whether they are relatively inefficient depends on comparative mean squared errors.'

Formal content, with every hypothesis. Let $h=1,2,3,\ldots$ index a sequence of finite populations with their randomization distributions (Section 3.3, p. 45), with parameters $\Delta_h$, and let $T_h$ and $U_h$ be real-valued estimators of $\Delta_h$ with finite second moments under the randomization distribution of population $h$ (automatic for a finite population). Write $b_h=\mathrm{E}[T_h]-\Delta_h$ and $\mathrm{MSE}(T_h)=\mathrm{E}[(T_h-\Delta_h)^2]$.
(a) For every $h$: $\mathrm{MSE}(T_h)=\mathrm{V}(T_h)+b_h^2\geq b_h^2$.
(b) If $b_h\to b$ with $b\neq0$ and $\mathrm{MSE}(U_h)\to0$ as $h\to\infty$, then there is $h_0$ such that $\mathrm{MSE}(U_h)<\mathrm{MSE}(T_h)$ for all $h\geq h_0$.
(c) For every $h$ and every $\varepsilon>0$: $P(|U_h-\Delta_h|>\varepsilon)\leq\mathrm{MSE}(U_h)/\varepsilon^2$; hence $\mathrm{MSE}(U_h)\to0$ implies $U_h-\Delta_h\to0$ in probability.
The hypothesis $\mathrm{MSE}(U_h)\to0$ in (b) cannot be dropped (see the counterexample target for this finding).
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: Bias: p. 42 (PDF p. 4), 'the difference between the expected value of the estimator (over all randomizations) and the parameter of interest'. Sequence of finite populations and consistency: p. 45 (PDF p. 7), 'Consistency of a statistic under a finite population is defined given a sequence of $h$ finite populations $H$ where $N_h<N_{h+1}$, $n_{th}<n_{th+1}$ and $n_{ch}<n_{ch+1}$ for $h=1,2,3,\ldots$. The estimator $\widehat{\Delta_S}$ is said to be a consistent estimator of $\Delta$ if $\widehat{\Delta_S}\xrightarrow{p}\Delta$ (converges in probability) as $h\to\infty$.' Mean squared error is not defined by a formula in the paper ('efficiency (typically mean square error)', p. 40); it is $\mathrm{E}[(T_h-\Delta_h)^2]$.
canonical_claim.finite_lemmas: For each fixed $h$: (a) the decomposition $\mathrm{MSE}(T_h)=\mathrm{V}(T_h)+b_h^2\geq b_h^2$; (c) the Markov (Chebyshev) bound $P(|U_h-\Delta_h|>\varepsilon)\leq\mathrm{MSE}(U_h)/\varepsilon^2$. The paper prints no derivation for this passage; both are in the validator's derivation.md, section 7.
canonical_claim.note: Finding rated Minor (error); repair cost recorded by the validator: weaker conclusion. Vanishing comparator MSE is sufficient, not necessary. Part (b) is a statement about sequences; parts (a) and (c) are its finite lemmas.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Appendix B, equation (31), with equations (29)-(30); the same formula is printed unnumbered at the end of p. 57 in Section 5.3
canonical_claim.statement:
As printed (pp. 70-71): 'Consider the situation where one wishes to improve upon the HT estimator by adjusting for cluster size; in other words, one wishes to estimate $k$ in equations 20 and 21 from the data to approximate the optimal value of $k$ with an estimator $\hat k$. In this scenario, the expected value of equation 20 yields ... (29) ... Likewise, ... (30) ... So the expected value of the estimator will be $\mathrm{E}\left[\frac{\widehat{Y^T_{1,R1}}-\widehat{Y^T_{0,R1}}}{N}\right]=\Delta+\frac MN(\mathrm{Cov}(\hat k,\overline{n_{cj}})-\mathrm{Cov}(\hat k,\overline{n_{cj}})).$ (31) The term on the right of equation 31 represents the bias.'

Corrected statement, with every hypothesis. Under random allocation of $m_t$ of the $M$ clusters to treatment ($0<m_t<M$, $m_c=M-m_t$), let $\hat k$ be an estimator of $k$ computed from the data of the same experiment, so that $\hat k$ is a random variable over randomizations and 'a constant for a given randomization', and let it replace $k$ in both equations 20 and 21: $\widehat{Y^T_{0,R1}}=\frac M{m_c}\sum_{j\in J_0}(Y^T_j-\hat k(n_j-N/M))$ and $\widehat{Y^T_{1,R1}}=\frac M{m_t}\sum_{j\in J_1}(Y^T_j-\hat k(n_j-N/M))$. Let $\overline{n_{tj}}=\frac1{m_t}\sum_{j\in J_1}n_j$ and $\overline{n_{cj}}=\frac1{m_c}\sum_{j\in J_0}n_j$, and let $\mathrm{E}$ and $\mathrm{Cov}$ be taken over the randomization distribution. Then
$\mathrm{E}\left[\widehat{Y^T_{1,R1}}\right]=\mathrm{E}\left[\frac M{m_t}\sum_{j\in J_1}(Y^T_j-\hat k(n_j-N/M))\right]=\frac M{m_t}\left(\mathrm{E}\left[\sum_{j\in J_1}Y^T_j\right]-\mathrm{E}\left[\sum_{j\in J_1}\hat kn_j\right]+\mathrm{E}\left[\sum_{j\in J_1}\hat kN/M\right]\right)=\frac M{m_t}\left(\mathrm{E}\left[m_t\overline{Y^T_{1j}}\right]-\mathrm{E}[\hat km_t\overline{n_{tj}}]+\mathrm{E}[\hat km_tN/M]\right)=Y^T_1-M(\mathrm{E}[\hat k\overline{n_{tj}}]-\mathrm{E}[\hat k]\mathrm{E}[\overline{n_{tj}}])=Y^T_1-M\mathrm{Cov}(\hat k,\overline{n_{tj}}),$ (29)
$\mathrm{E}\left[\widehat{Y^T_{0,R1}}\right]=Y^T_0-M\mathrm{Cov}(\hat k,\overline{n_{cj}}),$ (30)
and
$\mathrm{E}\left[\frac{\widehat{Y^T_{1,R1}}-\widehat{Y^T_{0,R1}}}{N}\right]=\Delta+\frac MN\left(\mathrm{Cov}(\hat k,\overline{n_{cj}})-\mathrm{Cov}(\hat k,\overline{n_{tj}})\right).$ (31, corrected: the second covariance is with $\overline{n_{tj}}$)
This is the formula already printed in Section 5.3 (p. 57): $\mathrm{E}\left[\frac{\widehat{Y^T_{1,R1}}-\widehat{Y^T_{0,R1}}}{N}\right]-\Delta=\frac MN(\mathrm{Cov}(\hat k,\overline{n_{cj}})-\mathrm{Cov}(\hat k,\overline{n_{tj}}))$.
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: Des Raj difference estimator, equations (20)-(21) and the display after (22), p. 54 (PDF p. 16): $\widehat{Y^T_{0,R1}}=\frac M{m_c}\sum_{j\in J_0}(Y^T_j-k(n_j-N/M))$, $\widehat{Y^T_{1,R1}}=\frac M{m_t}\sum_{j\in J_1}(Y^T_j-k(n_j-N/M))$, $\widehat{\Delta_{R1}}=\frac1N\left[\widehat{Y^T_{1,R1}}-\widehat{Y^T_{0,R1}}\right]$, with $k$ a constant fixed before analysis; differenced variable $U^T_j=Y^T_j-k(n_j-N/M)$ (p. 54), with potential versions $U^T_{0j}=Y^T_{0j}-k(n_j-N/M)$ and $U^T_{1j}=Y^T_{1j}-k(n_j-N/M)$ (used on pp. 55-56; the first display of Section 5.3, p. 56, shows $U^T_{0j}-\overline{U^T_{0j}}=Y^T_{0j}-k(n_j-N/M)-\overline{Y^T_{0j}}$). p. 58 (PDF p. 20): 'where $\hat k$ is an estimator of $k$, $\overline{n_{tj}}$ is the mean value of $n_j$ for clusters in the treatment condition in a given randomization and $\overline{n_{cj}}$ is the mean value of $n_j$ for units in the control condition in a given randomization.' p. 71 (PDF p. 33): 'In the third line of equation 29, $\hat k$ moves outside the summation operator because it is a constant for a given randomization.' In the third line of (29), $\overline{Y^T_{1j}}$ is the mean of the observed totals $Y^T_j$ over the treated clusters $j\in J_1$ of the given randomization, so that $\mathrm{E}[m_t\overline{Y^T_{1j}}]=m_tY^T_1/M$; also $\mathrm{E}[\overline{n_{tj}}]=\mathrm{E}[\overline{n_{cj}}]=N/M$. p. 57 (PDF p. 19) on $\hat k$: 'to try to estimate $k$ from the data, utilizing ordinary least squares on the observed data (perhaps controlling for $D_j$)'.
canonical_claim.note: Finding rated Minor (error; a duplicated subscript that makes the printed bias term identically zero). Equations (29) and (30) are correct as printed and are transcribed with the corrected (31). Slips of finding P020-E010 in the same passage, read as corrected here: p. 71 says 'the expected value of equation 20 yields' where equation 21 (the treatment-total estimator) is meant, and pp. 58 and 71 say 'for units in the control condition' where clusters are meant. Derivation: derivations.md, section E005. Not included: the Appendix B remark that there is no bias under the sharp null with equal numbers of clusters in the two arms, which is neither a headline claim nor a finding (a reader notes it holds for a k-hat unchanged when arm labels are swapped).

canonical_claim.statement:
Printed statement refuted: equation (31) as printed, $\mathrm{E}\left[\frac{\widehat{Y^T_{1,R1}}-\widehat{Y^T_{0,R1}}}{N}\right]=\Delta+\frac MN(\mathrm{Cov}(\hat k,\overline{n_{cj}})-\mathrm{Cov}(\hat k,\overline{n_{cj}}))$, whose right-hand side equals $\Delta$ for every $\hat k$.

Counterexample (validator, exact). $M=3$, $m_t=1$, $m_c=2$, $(n_1,n_2,n_3)=(1,2,3)$, $N=6$, $(Y^T_{01},Y^T_{02},Y^T_{03})=(0,0,0)$, $(Y^T_{11},Y^T_{12},Y^T_{13})=(0,0,3)$, so $\Delta=1/2$. Let $\hat k$ be the ordinary least squares slope of the observed cluster totals $Y^T_j$ on $n_j$ (with an intercept and no treatment indicator) over the three clusters, i.e. $\hat k=\sigma(n_j,Y^T_j)/\sigma^2(n_j)$ computed from the observed totals. Over the three equally likely assignments (treated cluster 1, 2, 3):
$\hat k=(0,0,3/2)$; $\overline{n_{tj}}=(1,2,3)$; $\overline{n_{cj}}=(5/2,2,3/2)$; $\frac1N\left[\widehat{Y^T_{1,R1}}-\widehat{Y^T_{0,R1}}\right]=(0,0,3/8)$ with $\hat k$ in place of $k$ in equations 20 and 21.
Hence $\mathrm{E}\left[\frac{\widehat{Y^T_{1,R1}}-\widehat{Y^T_{0,R1}}}{N}\right]=\frac18\neq\frac12=\Delta$: the bias is $-\frac38$, not $0$. Moreover $\mathrm{Cov}(\hat k,\overline{n_{tj}})=\frac12$, $\mathrm{Cov}(\hat k,\overline{n_{cj}})=-\frac14$ and $\frac MN\left(\mathrm{Cov}(\hat k,\overline{n_{cj}})-\mathrm{Cov}(\hat k,\overline{n_{tj}})\right)=\frac12\left(-\frac14-\frac12\right)=-\frac38$, in agreement with the corrected equation (31).

canonical_claim.location: pp. 48-49 (PDF pp. 10-11); Appendix A, p. 70 (PDF p. 32)
canonical_claim.statement:
(a) Unbiasedness, pp. 48-49: '$\widehat{Y^T_{0,HT}}=\frac M{m_c}\sum_{j\in J_0}Y^T_{0j}=\frac M{m_c}\sum_{j\in J_0}Y^T_j.$ (11) ... Likewise, $\widehat{Y^T_{1,HT}}=\frac M{m_t}\sum_{j\in J_1}Y^T_{1j}=\frac M{m_t}\sum_{j\in J_1}Y^T_j.$ (12) Following the same steps as equation 4, it can be shown that $\widehat{Y^T_{0,HT}}$ and $\widehat{Y^T_{1,HT}}$ are unbiased estimators of $Y_0^T$ and $Y_1^T$, respectively. ... From these two unbiased estimators, we may therefore construct an estimator of the ATE: $\widehat{\Delta_{HT}}=\frac1N\left[\widehat{Y^T_{1,HT}}-\widehat{Y^T_{0,HT}}\right]=\frac MN\left[\frac1{m_t}\sum_{j\in J_1}Y^T_j-\frac1{m_c}\sum_{j\in J_0}Y^T_j\right].$ (13)' With p. 42 ('If the estimators $\widehat{Y_0^T}$ and $\widehat{Y_1^T}$ are unbiased, the corresponding estimator of $\Delta$ is also unbiased'), the claim is: under random allocation of clusters, $\mathrm{E}[\widehat{Y^T_{0,HT}}]=Y_0^T$, $\mathrm{E}[\widehat{Y^T_{1,HT}}]=Y_1^T$ and $\mathrm{E}[\widehat{\Delta_{HT}}]=\Delta$.

(b) Non-invariance, p. 49: 'let $Y^*_{1ij}$ be a linear transformation of the treatment outcome for the $i^{th}$ person in the $j^{th}$ cluster such that $Y^*_{1ij}\equiv b_0+b_1\cdot Y_{1ij}$ and likewise, the control outcomes, $Y^*_{0ij}\equiv b_0+b_1\cdot Y_{0ij}$. Invariance to this transformation would imply that, when analyzing the transformed data, we achieve the relationship between the old estimate and new estimate such that $\widehat{\Delta^*_{HT}}=b_1\cdot\widehat{\Delta_{HT}},$ (14) ... In Appendix A, we demonstrate that the HT estimator is not location-invariant because the estimate based on the transformed data will be $\widehat{\Delta^*_{HT}}=b_0\cdot\frac MN\left[\frac1{m_t}\sum_{j\in J_1}n_j-\frac1{m_c}\sum_{j\in J_0}n_j\right]+b_1\cdot\widehat{\Delta_{HT}}.$ (15) Unless $b_0=0$, the term on the left does not generally reduce to zero but instead varies across treatment assignments, so equation 15 is not generally equivalent to equation 14 for a given randomization.'
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: Cluster totals and observed total: p. 48 (standing assumption S4). $\widehat{\Delta^*_{HT}}$ is the estimator (13) computed from the transformed outcomes, with $Y^{T*}_j=\sum_{i=1}^{n_j}Y^*_{ij}$ (Appendix A, p. 70, first two lines of the display: $\widehat{\Delta^*_{HT}}=\frac MN\left[\frac1{m_t}\sum_{j\in J_1}Y^{T*}_j-\frac1{m_c}\sum_{j\in J_0}Y^{T*}_j\right]=\frac MN\left[\frac1{m_t}\sum_{j\in J_1}\sum_{i=1}^{n_j}Y^*_{ij}-\frac1{m_c}\sum_{j\in J_0}\sum_{i=1}^{n_j}Y^*_{ij}\right]$). Equation (4), p. 43 (PDF p. 5), is the unit-level analogue: $\mathrm{E}\left[\widehat{Y^T_{0,S}}\right]=\mathrm{E}\left[\frac N{n_c}\sum_{i\in I_0}Y_i\right]=N\cdot\overline{Y_0}=Y_0^T$.
canonical_claim.note: Exact finite-sample statements. (15) is an identity for every assignment; the non-invariance claim is that (14) fails for some assignment whenever $b_0\neq0$ and $\frac1{m_t}\sum_{j\in J_1}n_j\neq\frac1{m_c}\sum_{j\in J_0}n_j$ (in (15) 'the term on the left' is the first term on the right-hand side). canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Equations (20)-(22) and the display that follows (Des Raj difference estimator, unbiased for fixed k); Section 5.4 estimators $\widehat{Y^T_{0,R2}}$, $\widehat{Y^T_{1,R2}}$, $\widehat{\Delta_{R2}}$ (covariate version, unbiased)
canonical_claim.statement:
(a) p. 54: '$\widehat{Y^T_{0,R1}}=\frac M{m_c}\sum_{j\in J_0}(Y^T_j-k(n_j-N/M)),$ (20) where constant $k$ is a prior estimate of the regression coefficient from a regression of $Y^T_j$ on $n_j$, and $(n_j-N/M)$ is the difference between the size of cluster $j$ and the average cluster size. ... Similarly, $\widehat{Y^T_{1,R1}}=\frac M{m_t}\sum_{j\in J_1}(Y^T_j-k(n_j-N/M)).$ (21) To develop an intuition about this method, note that it is equivalent to defining a new "differenced" variable $U^T_j$, where $U^T_j=Y^T_j-k(n_j-N/M)$ and conducting the analysis based on $U^T_j$ instead of $Y^T_j$. So long as $k$ is fixed before analysis, this strategy does not lead to bias because $\mathrm{E}k[n_j-N/M]=k\mathrm{E}[n_j-N/M]=k\cdot0=0.$ (22) It follows that the HT and Des Raj estimators have the same expected value. Since $\widehat{Y^T_{0,R1}}$ and $\widehat{Y^T_{1,R1}}$ are unbiased, it follows that the Des Raj estimator, $\widehat{\Delta_{R1}}=\frac1N\left[\widehat{Y^T_{1,R1}}-\widehat{Y^T_{0,R1}}\right],$ is also unbiased.' That is: under random allocation of clusters, for every constant $k$ fixed before analysis, $\mathrm{E}[\widehat{Y^T_{0,R1}}]=Y^T_0$, $\mathrm{E}[\widehat{Y^T_{1,R1}}]=Y^T_1$ and $\mathrm{E}[\widehat{\Delta_{R1}}]=\Delta$.

(b) pp. 58-59: 'Define the cluster total of the covariate, $X^T_{aj}=\sum_{i=1}^{n_j}X_{aij}$, and define the sum of the $X_{aij}$ across all individuals in all clusters, $X^T_a=\sum_{j=1}^M\sum_{i=1}^{n_j}X_{aij}$. ... Define constants $k'$ and $k_a$ ($\forall a$) as prior estimates of the coefficients associated with a regression of $Y_j$ on cluster size and cluster-level covariates, respectively. ... It follows that we may define $\widehat{Y^T_{0,R2}}=\frac M{m_c}\sum_{j\in J_0}\left(Y^T_j-k'(n_j-N/M)-\sum_{a=1}^Ak_a(X^T_{aj}-X^T_a/M)\right)$ and $\widehat{Y^T_{1,R2}}=\frac M{m_t}\sum_{j\in J_1}\left(Y^T_j-k'(n_j-N/M)-\sum_{a=1}^Ak_a(X^T_{aj}-X^T_a/M)\right).$ [the printed display for $\widehat{Y^T_{0,R2}}$ carries the underbrace labels 'adjusting for size' and 'adjusting for other covariates'] By the logic of equation 22, $\widehat{Y^T_{0,R2}}$ and $\widehat{Y^T_{1,R2}}$ are unbiased estimators of $Y^T_0$ and $Y^T_1$, respectively. It follows that we may again construct an unbiased estimator of $\Delta$, $\widehat{\Delta_{R2}}=\frac1N\left[\widehat{Y^T_{1,R2}}-\widehat{Y^T_{0,R2}}\right].$'
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: Cluster totals and observed total $Y^T_j$: p. 48 (standing assumption S4). Covariates, p. 58 (PDF p. 20): 'Assume the researcher has access to $A$ covariates for each individual $i$ in cluster $j$, denoted by $X^T_{aij}$, $a\in1,2,\ldots,A$' (the individual-level symbol is $X_{aij}$; the covariates are fixed, not affected by assignment). $k$, $k'$, $k_a$ are constants fixed before the randomization is analysed. HT estimator: equations (11)-(13).
canonical_claim.note: Exact finite-sample statements; this is the unbiasedness part of headline claim H6 (location invariance is the corrected equation (25) target; the bias from estimating k within sample is the corrected equation (31) target and its counterexample). Equation (22) is transcribed as printed; it is read as the expectation of $n_j-N/M$ for a uniformly selected cluster, equivalently $\mathrm{E}\left[\frac1{m_a}\sum_{j\in J_a}(n_j-N/M)\right]=0$ for each arm $a$ (candidate P020-E006 against this display was rated not confirmed; batch derivations.md, section E006). canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Equation (26), Section 5.3, and Appendix C (equation (32) to the final inequality): the variance-minimizing k and the comparison of the Des Raj estimator with the HT estimator
canonical_claim.location: pp. 56-57 (PDF pp. 18-19); Appendix C, pp. 71-73 (PDF pp. 33-35)
canonical_claim.statement:
(a) p. 56: 'To derive the optimal value of $k$, we begin by noting that the variance of $U^T_{0j}$ is $\sigma^2(U^T_{0j})=\frac{\sum_j\left(U^T_{0j}-\overline{U^T_{0j}}\right)^2}{M}=\frac{\sum_j\left(Y^T_{0j}-k(n_j-N/M)-\overline{Y^T_{0j}}\right)^2}{M}=\sigma^2(Y^T_{0j})+k^2\sigma^2(n_j)-2k\sigma(n_j,Y^T_{0j}),$ where $\overline{U^T_{0j}}$ is the mean value of $U^T_{0j}$ over all $j$ clusters. $k_{optim_c}$, the value of $k$ that minimizes $\sigma^2(U^T_{0j})$, can be found using simple optimization. Since the second derivative with respect to $k$, $2\sigma^2(n_j)$, must be positive, we may set the first derivative equal to zero and solve for $k$, so that $k_{optim_c}=\frac{\sigma(n_j,Y^T_{0j})}{\sigma^2(n_j)}.$ (26)' p. 57: 'Likewise, the optimal value of $k$ for the potential outcomes under treatment is $k_{optim_t}=\sigma(n_j,Y^T_{1j})/\sigma^2(n_j)$. ... In Appendix C, we derive a single optimal value of $k$, $k_{optim*}=m_tk_{optim_c}/M+m_ck_{optim_t}/M$.'

(b) Appendix C, pp. 71-73: 'To identify a single optimal value of $k$, $k_{optim*}$, we refer to the first line of equation 17, $v\mathrm{V}(\widehat{\Delta_{R1}})=c\sigma^2(U^T_{j0})+t\sigma^2(U^T_{j1})+2\sigma(U^T_{j0},U^T_{j1})$ (32) where $v=\frac{(M-1)N^2}{M^2}$, $c=\frac{M-m_c}{m_c}$, and $t=\frac{M-m_t}{m_t}$. ... Substituting equations 33, 34, and 35 into equation 32, $v\mathrm{V}(\widehat{\Delta_{R1}})=c[\sigma^2(Y^T_{j0})+k^2\sigma^2(n_j)-2k\sigma(Y^T_{j0},n_j)]+t[\sigma^2(Y^T_{j1})+k^2\sigma^2(n_j)-2k\sigma(Y^T_{j1},n_j)]+2[\sigma(Y^T_{j0},Y^T_{j1})-k\sigma(Y^T_{j0},n_j)-k\sigma(Y^T_{j1},n_j)+k^2\sigma^2(n_j)].$ Setting the first derivative with respect to $k$ equal to zero,
$0=c[2k_{optim*}\sigma^2(n_j)-2\sigma(Y^T_{j0},n_j)]+t[2k_{optim*}\sigma^2(n_j)-2\sigma(Y^T_{j1},n_j)]+2[-\sigma(Y^T_{j0},n_j)-\sigma(Y^T_{j1},n_j)+2k_{optim*}\sigma^2(n_j)],$
$ck_{optim*}\sigma^2(n_j)+tk_{optim*}\sigma^2(n_j)+2k_{optim*}\sigma^2(n_j)=c\sigma(Y^T_{j0},n_j)+t\sigma(Y^T_{j1},n_j)+\sigma(Y^T_{j0},n_j)+\sigma(Y^T_{j1},n_j)$
$\left(\frac{M-m_c}{m_c}+\frac{M-m_t}{m_t}+\frac{m_c}{m_c}+\frac{m_t}{m_t}\right)k_{optim*}\sigma^2(n_j)=\left(\frac{M-m_c}{m_c}+\frac{m_c}{m_c}\right)\cdot\sigma(Y^T_{j0},n_j)+\left(\frac{M-m_t}{m_t}+\frac{m_t}{m_t}\right)\cdot\sigma(Y^T_{j1},n_j)$
$\left(\frac M{m_c}+\frac M{m_t}\right)k_{optim*}\sigma^2(n_j)=\left(\frac M{m_c}\right)\sigma(Y^T_{j0},n_j)+\left(\frac M{m_t}\right)\sigma(Y^T_{j1},n_j)$
$k_{optim*}=\left(\frac1{m_c}+\frac1{m_t}\right)^{-1}\left[\left(\frac1{m_c}\right)\frac{\sigma(Y^T_{j0},n_j)}{\sigma^2(n_j)}+\left(\frac1{m_t}\right)\frac{\sigma(Y^T_{j1},n_j)}{\sigma^2(n_j)}\right]$
$k_{optim*}=\left(\frac1{m_c}+\frac1{m_t}\right)^{-1}\left[\left(\frac1{m_c}\right)k_{optim_c}+\left(\frac1{m_t}\right)k_{optim_t}\right]$
$k_{optim*}=\frac{m_t}Mk_{optim_c}+\frac{m_c}Mk_{optim_t}.$
The Des Raj estimator will be more efficient than the HT estimator when
$(c+t+2)k^2\sigma^2(n_j)<2k[(c+1)\sigma(Y^T_{j0},n_j)+(t+1)\sigma(Y^T_{j1},n_j)]$
$(c+t+2)k^2<2k\left[(c+1)\frac{\sigma(Y^T_{j0},n_j)}{\sigma^2(n_j)}+(t+1)\frac{\sigma(Y^T_{j1},n_j)}{\sigma^2(n_j)}\right]$
$(c+t+2)k^2<2k[(c+1)k_{optim_c}+(t+1)k_{optim_t}]$
$k^2<2k\left[\frac{m_t}Mk_{optim_c}+\frac{m_c}Mk_{optim_t}\right]$
$k^2<2k\cdot k_{optim*}.$'

(c) p. 57: 'The chosen value of $k$ will reduce the variability of the Des Raj estimator, $\widehat{\Delta_{R1}}$, relative to the HT estimator when, for $k_{optim*}>0$, $0<k<2k_{optim*}$ and, for $k_{optim*}<0$, $0>k>2k_{optim*}$.'
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: Des Raj difference estimator, equations (20)-(21) and the display after (22), p. 54 (PDF p. 16): $\widehat{Y^T_{0,R1}}=\frac M{m_c}\sum_{j\in J_0}(Y^T_j-k(n_j-N/M))$, $\widehat{Y^T_{1,R1}}=\frac M{m_t}\sum_{j\in J_1}(Y^T_j-k(n_j-N/M))$, $\widehat{\Delta_{R1}}=\frac1N\left[\widehat{Y^T_{1,R1}}-\widehat{Y^T_{0,R1}}\right]$, with $k$ a constant fixed before analysis; differenced variable $U^T_j=Y^T_j-k(n_j-N/M)$ (p. 54), with potential versions $U^T_{0j}=Y^T_{0j}-k(n_j-N/M)$ and $U^T_{1j}=Y^T_{1j}-k(n_j-N/M)$ (used on pp. 55-56; the first display of Section 5.3, p. 56, shows $U^T_{0j}-\overline{U^T_{0j}}=Y^T_{0j}-k(n_j-N/M)-\overline{Y^T_{0j}}$). Finite population variance and covariance with divisor $M$, p. 50 (PDF p. 12) (standing assumption S5). Appendix C writes $Y^T_{j0}$, $Y^T_{j1}$, $U^T_{j0}$, $U^T_{j1}$ for the main text's $Y^T_{0j}$, $Y^T_{1j}$, $U^T_{0j}$, $U^T_{1j}$. 'The first line of equation 17' (p. 51, PDF p. 13), applied to the differenced totals: $\mathrm{V}(\widehat{\Delta_{HT}})=\frac1{N^2}\left[\frac{M^2}{m_c}\left(\frac{M-m_c}{M-1}\right)\sigma^2(Y^T_{0j})+\frac{M^2}{m_t}\left(\frac{M-m_t}{M-1}\right)\sigma^2(Y^T_{1j})+\frac{2M^2}{M-1}\sigma(Y^T_{0j},Y^T_{1j})\right]$. Equations (33)-(35): see the corrected-statement target for Appendix C. 'More efficient' means $\mathrm{V}(\widehat{\Delta_{R1}})<\mathrm{V}(\widehat{\Delta_{HT}})$, the HT estimator being the case $k=0$ (p. 56).
canonical_claim.note: Exact finite-sample statements, transcribed as printed. The divisions by $\sigma^2(n_j)$ and the phrase 'must be positive' presuppose unequal cluster sizes: P020-E007 is rated a clarity note (not an error) for the missing hypothesis $\sigma^2(n_j)>0$ and for the informal paraphrase on p. 57 that drops the equality cases. The formal content, in the batch validator's form (derivations.md, section E007): for $\sigma^2(n_j)>0$, $v[\mathrm{V}(\widehat{\Delta_{R1}})-\mathrm{V}(\widehat{\Delta_{HT}})]=(c+t+2)\sigma^2(n_j)\,k(k-2k_{optim*})$, so $k_{optim*}$ is the unique minimizer, the Des Raj variance is strictly smaller than the HT variance iff $k^2<2k\cdot k_{optim*}$, and the two are equal at $k=0$ and $k=2k_{optim*}$; if all clusters have equal size every $k$ gives the HT estimator. The rest of headline claim H7 ('adjustment ... can therefore improve precision') is a qualitative consequence and not a separate target.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Equations (16)-(17), $\mathrm{V}_{apx}$ and the estimator $\hat{\mathrm{V}}(\widehat{\Delta_{HT}})$ (Section 4.2); equations (18)-(19) (block designs, Section 4.3); equation (23) (Des Raj version, Section 5.1)
canonical_claim.statement:
(a) p. 50: 'The variance of the estimator in equation 13 is $\mathrm{V}(\hat\Delta)=\frac1{N^2}\left[\mathrm{V}\left(\widehat{Y^T_0}\right)+\mathrm{V}\left(\widehat{Y^T_1}\right)-2\mathrm{Cov}\left(\widehat{Y^T_0},\widehat{Y^T_1}\right)\right].$ (16) ... From the principles of finite population sampling, $\mathrm{V}\left(\widehat{Y^T_{0,HT}}\right)=\frac{M^2}{m_c}\left(\frac{M-m_c}{M-1}\right)\sigma^2(Y^T_{0j}),$ $\mathrm{V}\left(\widehat{Y^T_{1,HT}}\right)=\frac{M^2}{m_t}\left(\frac{M-m_t}{M-1}\right)\sigma^2(Y^T_{1j}),$ and $\mathrm{Cov}\left(\widehat{Y^T_{0,HT}},\widehat{Y^T_{1,HT}}\right)=-\frac{M^2}{M-1}\sigma(Y^T_{0j},Y^T_{1j})$'.

(b) p. 51: 'From equation 16, $\mathrm{V}(\widehat{\Delta_{HT}})=\frac1{N^2}\left[\frac{M^2}{m_c}\left(\frac{M-m_c}{M-1}\right)\sigma^2(Y^T_{0j})+\frac{M^2}{m_t}\left(\frac{M-m_t}{M-1}\right)\sigma^2(Y^T_{1j})+\frac{2M^2}{M-1}\sigma(Y^T_{0j},Y^T_{1j})\right]=\frac{M^2}{N^2}\left[\frac M{M-1}\left[\frac{\sigma^2(Y^T_{0j})}{m_c}+\frac{\sigma^2(Y^T_{1j})}{m_t}\right]+\frac1{M-1}[2\sigma(Y^T_{0j},Y^T_{1j})-\sigma^2(Y^T_{0j})-\sigma^2(Y^T_{1j})]\right].$ (17)'

(c) p. 51: 'Since $2\sigma(Y^T_{0j},Y^T_{1j})-\sigma^2(Y^T_{0j})-\sigma^2(Y^T_{1j})\leq0$, it follows that $\mathrm{V}(\widehat{\Delta_{HT}})\leq\mathrm{V}_{apx}\left(\widehat{\Delta_{HT}}\right)=\frac{M^3}{N^2(M-1)}\left[\frac{\sigma^2(Y^T_{0j})}{m_c}+\frac{\sigma^2(Y^T_{1j})}{m_t}\right].$'

(d) p. 51: 'Substituting unbiased estimators of $\sigma^2(Y^T_{0j})$ and $\sigma^2(Y^T_{1j})$ (Cochran 1977, theorem 2.4), we may derive an unbiased estimator of the quantity $\mathrm{V}_{apx}(\widehat{\Delta_{HT}})$, $\hat{\mathrm{V}}(\widehat{\Delta_{HT}})=\frac{M^2}{N^2}\left[\frac{\sum_{j\in J_0}\left(Y^T_j-\overline{Y^T_{cj}}\right)^2}{m_c(m_c-1)}+\frac{\sum_{j\in J_1}\left(Y^T_j-\overline{Y^T_{tj}}\right)^2}{m_t(m_t-1)}\right],$ where $\overline{Y^T_{mj}}=\sum_{j\in J_0}Y^T_j/m_c$, the mean value of $Y^T_j$ over all $j\in J_0$ and $\overline{Y^T_{tj}}=\sum_{j\in J_1}Y^T_j/m_t$, the mean value of $Y^T_j$ over all $j\in J_1$. The bias of the variance estimator is always nonnegative, thus ensuring the variance estimator is conservative. ... In addition, when $m_c$ or $m_t$ is 1 the estimate is undefined.' That is: for $m_c\geq2$ and $m_t\geq2$, $\mathrm{E}[\hat{\mathrm{V}}(\widehat{\Delta_{HT}})]=\mathrm{V}_{apx}(\widehat{\Delta_{HT}})\geq\mathrm{V}(\widehat{\Delta_{HT}})$.

(e) p. 55, Des Raj version: 'Deriving a conservative estimator of the variance of the Des Raj estimator follows directly from Section 4.2: $\hat{\mathrm{V}}(\widehat{\Delta_{R1}})=\frac{M^2}{N^2}\left[\frac{\sum_{j\in J_0}\left(U^T_j-\overline{U^T_{cj}}\right)^2}{m_c(m_c-1)}+\frac{\sum_{j\in J_1}\left(U^T_j-\overline{U^T_{tj}}\right)^2}{m_t(m_t-1)}\right],$ (23) where $\overline{U^T_{cj}}=\sum_{j\in J_0}U^T_j/m_c$, the mean value of $U^T_j$ in the control condition and $\overline{U^T_{tj}}=\sum_{j\in J_1}U^T_j/m_t$, the mean value of $U^T_j$ in the treatment condition.'

(f) p. 53, block designs: 'In the $b^{th}$ block, a fixed number of clusters, $m_{tb}$, are assigned to treatment and the rest, $m_{cb}$, to control. As each block represents an independent randomized experiment, the HT estimator and variance estimators may be applied to each block separately. For the $b^{th}$ block the estimator of the ATE can be written $\widehat{\Delta^b_{HT}}$. An unbiased estimate of the ATE for all the units in the study can be written as a weighted average of the block-level estimates, $\widehat{\Delta^B_{HT}}=\sum_{b=1}^B\frac{N_b}N\widehat{\Delta^b_{HT}},$ (18) where $N_b$ is the number of units in the $b^{th}$ block. From first principles, the variance of the estimator is $\mathrm{V}\left(\widehat{\Delta^B_{HT}}\right)=\sum_{b=1}^B\frac{N_b^2}{N^2}\mathrm{V}\left(\widehat{\Delta^b_{HT}}\right),$ (19) and conservative variance estimation can be achieved by "plugging in" conservative estimators of the variance for each of the $\mathrm{V}\left(\widehat{\Delta^b_{HT}}\right)$.'

The control-arm mean in the display of (d) is $\overline{Y^T_{cj}}=\sum_{j\in J_0}Y^T_j/m_c$ (the 'where' clause prints the subscript as $mj$; see note). canonical_claim.note: Exact finite-sample statements, transcribed as printed; both readers re-derived (a)-(d) and confirmed them by exact enumeration. The unbiasedness in (d) needs $m_c\geq2$ and $m_t\geq2$, as the paper says, and uses $\mathrm{E}\left[\frac1{m_c-1}\sum_{j\in J_0}(Y^T_j-\overline{Y^T_{cj}})^2\right]=\frac M{M-1}\sigma^2(Y^T_{0j})$ and the same for the treatment arm. (e) is (d) applied to $U^T_j$ for fixed $k$. The sharp-null variance and its exactness under no effect are in the P020-N001 corrected-statement target; its conservativeness is in the next target.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Section 4.2, unnumbered statement that the sharp-null variance estimator $\hat{\mathrm{V}}^N(\widehat{\Delta_{HT}})$ is conservative if effects are constant at the cluster scale or if the number of clusters is balanced
canonical_claim.location: p. 52 (PDF p. 14); explicit form on p. 52 and, for the Des Raj estimator, p. 55 (PDF p. 17)
canonical_claim.statement:
As printed (p. 52): 'When the sharp null hypothesis of no effect does not necessarily hold, $\mathrm{V}^N(\widehat{\Delta_{HT}})$ may be construed as an estimator of $\mathrm{V}(\widehat{\Delta_{HT}})$. We therefore refer to a variance estimator constructed by assuming the sharp null hypothesis of no effect as $\hat{\mathrm{V}}^N(\widehat{\Delta_{HT}})$.' and 'In general, $\hat{\mathrm{V}}^N(\widehat{\Delta_{HT}})$ will be conservative relative to the true variance if effects are constant (at the cluster scale) or if the number of clusters is balanced, in a result that directly follows from theorem 3 of Ding (2014) and Samii and Aronow (2012) (by way of the relationship between pooled and combined variance). These results indicate $\hat{\mathrm{V}}^N(\widehat{\Delta_{HT}})$ will have a higher value than that of the true variance if treatment effects are in fact constant at the cluster scale.'

Formal reading (with 'conservative' as defined on p. 51: the bias of the variance estimator is nonnegative). Under random allocation of $m_t$ of the $M$ clusters to treatment ($0<m_t<M$, $m_c=M-m_t$), let $\hat{\mathrm{V}}^N(\widehat{\Delta_{HT}})=\frac{M^4\sigma^2(Y^T_j)}{N^2(M-1)m_cm_t}$, where $\sigma^2(Y^T_j)$ is the finite population variance (divisor $M$) of the observed cluster totals $Y^T_j=D_jY^T_{1j}+(1-D_j)Y^T_{0j}$. Then $\mathrm{E}\left[\hat{\mathrm{V}}^N(\widehat{\Delta_{HT}})\right]\geq\mathrm{V}(\widehat{\Delta_{HT}})$ if (i) the cluster-level effect $Y^T_{1j}-Y^T_{0j}$ is the same for every cluster $j$, or (ii) $m_c=m_t$.
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: Horvitz-Thompson estimator, equations (11)-(13), pp. 48-49 (PDF pp. 10-11): $\widehat{Y^T_{0,HT}}=\frac M{m_c}\sum_{j\in J_0}Y^T_j$, $\widehat{Y^T_{1,HT}}=\frac M{m_t}\sum_{j\in J_1}Y^T_j$, $\widehat{\Delta_{HT}}=\frac1N\left[\widehat{Y^T_{1,HT}}-\widehat{Y^T_{0,HT}}\right]=\frac MN\left[\frac1{m_t}\sum_{j\in J_1}Y^T_j-\frac1{m_c}\sum_{j\in J_0}Y^T_j\right]$. Finite population variance and covariance with divisor $M$, p. 50 (PDF p. 12) (standing assumption S5). $\mathrm{V}^N(\widehat{\Delta_{HT}})=\frac{M^4\sigma^2(Y^T_j)}{N^2(M-1)m_cm_t}$ (p. 52, PDF p. 14); the estimator computes it from the observed totals, as the paper's Des Raj version makes explicit (p. 55, PDF p. 17): $\hat{\mathrm{V}}^N(\widehat{\Delta_{R1}})=\frac{M^4\sigma^2(U^T_j)}{N^2(M-1)m_cm_t}$. True variance $\mathrm{V}(\widehat{\Delta_{HT}})$: equation (17), p. 51 (PDF p. 13). 'Constant (at the cluster scale)' is read as a constant cluster-total effect $Y^T_{1j}-Y^T_{0j}$; 'the number of clusters is balanced' as $m_c=m_t$.
canonical_claim.note: Exact finite-sample inequality in expectation; the paper gives no derivation and attributes it to Ding (2014) and Samii and Aronow (2012), which were not staged. P020-E009 is rated a clarity note (not an error): 'will have a higher value than that of the true variance' is the in-expectation property and need not hold for a realized assignment (validator's instance: $M=N=4$, $m_t=m_c=2$, $Y^T_{0j}=(0,0,2,2)$, $Y^T_{1j}=Y^T_{0j}+2$; true variance 4/3, mean of the estimator 8/3, one assignment gives 0). Exact expressions from the batch validator (derivations.md, section E009) and the Opus reader, with $d_j=Y^T_{1j}-Y^T_{0j}$: if $d_j=\tau$ for all $j$, $\mathrm{E}[\hat{\mathrm{V}}^N]-\mathrm{V}=\frac{M^2}{N^2(M-1)}\tau^2$; if $m_c=m_t$, $\mathrm{E}[\hat{\mathrm{V}}^N]-\mathrm{V}=\frac{M^2}{N^2(M-1)}\left[\bar d^{\,2}+\frac{M-2}{M-1}\sigma^2(d_j)\right]$. Both follow from $\mathrm{E}[\sigma^2(Y^T_j)]=p\sigma^2(Y^T_{1j})+q\sigma^2(Y^T_{0j})+pq\bar d^{\,2}-pq\sigma^2(d_j)/(M-1)$ with $p=m_t/M$, $q=m_c/M$. A reader notes that a constant individual-level effect with unequal cluster sizes is not a constant cluster-total effect and does not qualify.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Section 3.3, equation (9) (consistency of the difference-in-means estimator as the number of clusters grows) and equation (10) (the estimate is unchanged when cluster sizes grow with the number of clusters fixed)
canonical_claim.location: pp. 45-47 (PDF pp. 7-9); Figure 1 on p. 46 (PDF p. 8)
canonical_claim.statement:
(a) Definition, p. 45: 'Consistency of a statistic under a finite population is defined given a sequence of $h$ finite populations $H$ where $N_h<N_{h+1}$, $n_{th}<n_{th+1}$ and $n_{ch}<n_{ch+1}$ for $h=1,2,3,\ldots$. The estimator $\widehat{\Delta_S}$ is said to be a consistent estimator of $\Delta$ if $\widehat{\Delta_S}\xrightarrow{p}\Delta$ (converges in probability) as $h\to\infty$.'

(b) Growing number of clusters, pp. 46-47: 'To show that the difference-in-means estimator is consistent with large $M$, we follow Brewer (1979) in assuming that as $h\to\infty$, the finite population $H$ increases as follows: (1) the original population of $M$ clusters is exactly copied $(h-1)$ times; (2) from each of the $h$ copies, $m_t$ clusters are allocated to treatment (such that $0<m_t<M$) and the remaining $m_c=M-m_t$ are allocated to control; (3) the $h$ subsets are collected in a single population of $hM$ clusters, with $hm_t$ clusters in treatment and $hm_c=hM-hm_t$ in control; and (4) $\widehat{\Delta_S}$ is defined as the difference-in-means estimator as in equation 5, only now summation takes place across all $hm_c$ and $hm_t$ clusters. ... We express the estimator as, $\widehat{\Delta_S}=\sum_{j\in J_1}\sum_{i=1}^{n_j}Y_{ij}/\sum_{j\in J_1}n_j-\sum_{j\in J_0}\sum_{i=1}^{n_j}Y_{ij}/\sum_{j\in J_0}n_j$, where in this case $J_1$ is defined as the set of $hm_t$ treatment clusters and $J_0$ is defined as the set of $hm_c$ control clusters. As $h\to\infty$, by the weak law of large numbers, $\frac1h\sum_{j\in J_1}\sum_{i=1}^{n_j}Y_{ij}\xrightarrow{p}Y_1^T\cdot\frac{hm_t}{hM}$, $\frac1h\sum_{j\in J_0}\sum_{i=1}^{n_j}Y_{ij}\xrightarrow{p}Y_0^T\cdot\frac{hm_c}{hM}$, $\frac1h\sum_{j\in J_1}n_j\xrightarrow{p}N\cdot\frac{hm_t}{hM}$ and $\frac1h\sum_{j\in J_0}n_j\xrightarrow{p}N\cdot\frac{hm_c}{hM}$. By Slutsky's theorem, $\widehat{\Delta_S}\xrightarrow{p}\frac{Y_1^T\cdot\frac{hm_t}{hM}}{N\cdot\frac{hm_t}{hM}}-\frac{Y_0^T\cdot\frac{hm_c}{hM}}{N\cdot\frac{hm_c}{hM}}=\frac{Y_1^T-Y_0^T}N.$ (9)' 'This proves that the difference-in-means estimator is consistent as the number of clusters grows.'

(c) Growing cluster sizes, p. 47: 'In the case where the size (rather than the number) of the clusters grows as $h\to\infty$, the finite population $H$ increases as follows: (1) the original population of $M$ units is exactly copied $(h-1)$ times, but this time the $h$ copies of a cluster are considered part of one supercluster; (2) $m_t$ of the clusters are allocated to treatment (such that $0<m_t<M$) and the remaining $m_c=M-m_t$ are allocated to control; and (3) $\widehat{\Delta_S}$ is defined as the difference-in-means estimator as in equation 9, but now the inner summation takes place across all $hn_j$ units in each cluster. ... To show that the difference-in-means estimator is not necessarily consistent simply with large $N$, we express the estimator as, $\widehat{\Delta_S}=\frac{\sum_{j\in J_1}\sum_{i=1}^{hn_j}Y_{ij}}{\sum_{j\in J_1}hn_j}-\frac{\sum_{j\in J_0}\sum_{i=1}^{hn_j}Y_{ij}}{\sum_{j\in J_0}hn_j}=\frac{\sum_{j\in J_1}\sum_{i=1}^{n_j}Y_{ij}}{\sum_{j\in J_1}n_j}-\frac{\sum_{j\in J_0}\sum_{i=1}^{n_j}Y_{ij}}{\sum_{j\in J_0}n_j}.$ (10) As $h\to\infty$, the estimate remains unchanged with large $N$ if the number of clusters is fixed. This proves that the bias articulated in equation 8 is unmitigated for increasingly large clusters.'
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: Difference-in-means estimator, equation (6), p. 44 (PDF p. 6): $\widehat{\Delta_S}=\frac1N\left[\widehat{Y^T_{1,S}}-\widehat{Y^T_{0,S}}\right]=\frac{\sum_{j\in J_1}\sum_{i=1}^{n_j}Y_{ij}}{\sum_{j\in J_1}n_j}-\frac{\sum_{j\in J_0}\sum_{i=1}^{n_j}Y_{ij}}{\sum_{j\in J_0}n_j}$. In (b), $Y_1^T$, $Y_0^T$, $N$, $M$, $m_t$, $m_c$ are those of the original population ($h=1$); the allocation is carried out separately and independently within each of the $h$ copies, each copy allocating $m_t$ of its $M$ clusters to treatment. In (c), cluster $j$ of population $h$ consists of $h$ copies of each individual of the original cluster $j$, so its size is $hn_j$ and its potential totals are $hY^T_{0j}$, $hY^T_{1j}$; $M$ and $m_t$ are fixed. Figure 1 (p. 46): 'In Panel A, copies of the clusters are made and the number of clusters grows. In Panel B, the number of clusters is fixed and the individuals within are copied.' The ATE of every replicated population equals $\Delta=\frac{Y_1^T-Y_0^T}N$ of the original.
canonical_claim.finite_lemmas: (1) For one copy of the original population under random allocation of $m_t$ of its $M$ clusters (the means in the four weak-law limits on p. 46): $\mathrm{E}\left[\sum_{j\in J_1}Y^T_{1j}\right]=Y_1^T\cdot\frac{m_t}M$, $\mathrm{E}\left[\sum_{j\in J_0}Y^T_{0j}\right]=Y_0^T\cdot\frac{m_c}M$, $\mathrm{E}\left[\sum_{j\in J_1}n_j\right]=N\cdot\frac{m_t}M$, $\mathrm{E}\left[\sum_{j\in J_0}n_j\right]=N\cdot\frac{m_c}M$; across the $h$ copies the per-copy sums are independent, identically distributed and bounded, so each of the four quantities $\frac1h\sum(\cdot)$ is an average of $h$ such terms. (2) The algebraic identity on the right of equation (9), p. 46: $\frac{Y_1^T\cdot\frac{hm_t}{hM}}{N\cdot\frac{hm_t}{hM}}-\frac{Y_0^T\cdot\frac{hm_c}{hM}}{N\cdot\frac{hm_c}{hM}}=\frac{Y_1^T-Y_0^T}N$, with nonzero denominators since $0<m_t<M$ and $N>0$. (3) Equation (10), p. 47, is an exact identity for every $h\geq1$ and every assignment (the factor $h$ cancels in each ratio); hence in the Panel-B sequence the randomization distribution of $\widehat{\Delta_S}$, its expectation and its bias (equation 8) are the same for every $h$, while $\Delta$ is also the same for every $h$.
canonical_claim.note: Asymptotic headline result. (b) is a convergence-in-probability statement along the Brewer replication sequence; state it as such and prove the finite lemmas. (c) is exact for each h: its content is that consistency can fail when only cluster sizes grow, i.e. whenever the bias (8) of the original population is nonzero the estimator does not converge in probability to $\Delta$ (an instance with nonzero bias is in the P020-E001 counterexample target). Slips of finding P020-E010 in (c), read as corrected: 'the original population of $M$ units' means $M$ clusters, and 'as in equation 9' means the estimator of equation 6. In (b), item (4) cites equation 5, whose cluster form is equation 6. Both readers followed each step and recorded the result as holding for the stated replication asymptotics.
